evidence.title: The "DeepSeek effect" and the adoption-integration gap of generative artificial intelligence in clinical practice: a national online convenience cross-sectional survey of academic critical care physicians in China
evidence.outcome: Self-reported professional competence with structured GAI training covering risks, verification, ethics
evidence.effect: Structured training associated with improved self-reported competence (AOR 22.2, 95% CI 1.6–305.6, p=0.021; n=15, exploratory); any training AOR 1.98 (1.37–2.86); 86.7% vs 28.6% prioritized critical appraisal skills (OR 16.3).
evidence.quote: Multivariate analysis adjusted for demographic factors revealed a significant association between structured training and perceived improvement in self-reported professional competence (AOR = 22.2, 95% CI: 1.6–305.6, p = 0.021).

evidence.title: Boosting LLM-Assisted Diagnosis: 10-Minute LLM Tutorial Elevates Radiology Residents’ Performance in Brain MRI Interpretation
evidence.outcome: Top-three differential diagnosis accuracy, confidence, and reading time
evidence.effect: Correct diagnosis in top three was 62.5% (55/88) post-tutorial vs 44.8% (39/87) pre-tutorial (binary p=0.042, numeric p=0.016), with higher confidence (p=0.006) and no reading time difference.
evidence.quote: The LLM tutorial led to significantly higher performance (binary scores: p = 0.042, numeric scores: p = 0.016) and confidence (p = 0.006) but resulted in no relevant differences in reading times.

evidence.title: Increasing Generative Artificial Intelligence Competency among Students Enrolled in Doctoral Nursing Research Coursework
evidence.outcome: Self-rated generative AI competency after brief didactic and lab training on ChatGPT use and limitations
evidence.effect: All 10 students reported increasing self-rated generative AI competency by one to two points on a five-point scale; they identified strengths and limitations of ChatGPT across three tasks.
evidence.quote: All of them reported increasing their self-rated competency in generative AI by one to two points on a five-point rating scale.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of Informed AI Use on Clinical Competence of General Practitioners and Internists: Pre-Post Intervention Study
evidence.outcome: clinical decision-making test performance with generative AI
evidence.effect: After tailored AI training with GPT-4 use permitted, scores improved from 56.88% to 77.56%, mean difference 20.68%; P<.001.
evidence.quote: The mean score improved from 56.88% (SD 15.65%) to 77.56% (SD 12.71%), with a mean difference of 20.68% ( P <.001).
evidence.country: Multinational (39 countries; highest participation from Saudi Arabia, Syria, Egypt, Algeria, Jordan)

evidence.title: Changes in artificial intelligence literacy, attitudes, and acceptance following ChatGPT-based training among midwifery students
evidence.outcome: AI literacy, attitudes, and generative AI acceptance after 45-minute ChatGPT training
evidence.effect: AI literacy 59.94 to 61.25, not significant (p=0.351, d=0.17); acceptance 72.97 to 76.88 (p=0.008, d=0.51); attitudes 62.94 to 71.16 (p<0.001, d=0.96). No control group.
evidence.quote: Statistical analysis showed that there was no significant difference between the pre- and post-training scores on the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale ( p = 0.351).

evidence.title: Integrating Generative AI Into Clinical Reasoning Education for Medical Students: Mixed Methods Study
evidence.outcome: Self-perceived AI literacy (knowledge, application, evaluation, ethics) before vs after GenAI workshop
evidence.effect: Total score 3.57 to 4.23 (d=0.98, P<.001); domain effects d=0.69-0.93, all significant after FDR correction; self-reported only, no comparator, no performance measure.
evidence.quote: Self-perceived AI literacy improved across all domains (Cohen d=0.69-0.93, all P<.001; all remaining significant after false discovery rate correction), and collaborative learning attitudes increased substantially (d=0.94, P<.001).

evidence.title: Development and Effects of a Metaverse-Based Generative AI Nursing Informatics Competency Education Program for Clinical Nurses
evidence.outcome: Self-reported nursing informatics competency and ethical awareness of AI use
evidence.effect: The six-week generative AI education program improved nursing informatics competency more than control (p < 0.01), sustained at 4 weeks. Ethical awareness of AI use, self-efficacy, and EBP also improved (all p < 0.01), but these were unadjusted for multiplicity.
evidence.quote: Compared with the control group, the intervention group demonstrated a significantly greater improvement in nursing informatics competency, the pre-specified primary outcome (p < 0.01), sustained at the four-week follow-up.

evidence.title: The Use of Large Language Models in Postgraduate Plastic Surgery Training: A National Survey of Plastic Surgery Residents
evidence.outcome: Proportion of residents using LLMs who had received formal LLM education or training
evidence.effect: 94.4% reported not having received education or training on LLM use; 83.3% used LLMs for any purpose and 37.1% had concerns about using them for learning.
evidence.quote: Of respondents, 94.4% reported not having received education or training on the use of LLMs, and 37.1% reported concerns with the use of the technology for plastic surgery learning.

evidence.title: Medical students' use of large language models: a national survey
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of formal instruction on LLM use among medical students
evidence.effect: Formal instruction on LLM use was uncommon (10.95%), while 90.18% encountered inaccurate information; 67.67% agreed schools should integrate formal instruction.
evidence.quote: Formal instruction on LLM use was uncommon (10.95%), though 67.67% of students agreed medical schools should integrate formal instruction on LLMs.

evidence.title: AI in obstetrics: Evaluating residents' capabilities and interaction strategies with ChatGPT
evidence.venue: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology
evidence.outcome: Relationship between self-assessed AI skills and accuracy of ChatGPT responses
evidence.effect: No correlation between AI response accuracy and self-assessed IT or AI skills; most residents dissatisfied with AI training; perceived versus actual AI proficiency discrepancy.
evidence.quote: No correlation was found between AI response accuracy and the residents' self-assessed IT or AI skills, with most expressing dissatisfaction with their AI training.

commentary.bottom_line: Seven studies suggest that generative AI training may raise clinicians' and students' self-rated competence and, in two small or confounded tests, their performance on simulated tasks. No study measured whether training reduces staff misuse of generative AI or reliance on fabricated content in practice, so the recommendation rests mainly on expert endorsement and documented training gaps.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial of 46 nurses and six observational or pre-post studies test training, mostly with self-reported outcomes in simulated settings. In the 326-physician study, scores rose from 56.88% to 77.56%, but GPT-4 access changed at the same time as training. Indirect outcomes, small samples, and missing comparators lower certainty to very low.

Nine radiology residents placed the correct diagnosis in their top three 62.5% of the time after a tutorial versus 44.8% before. This suggests training may improve accuracy in simulation. Obstetrics residents' self-assessed AI skill did not correlate with the accuracy of AI responses, so gains in self-rated competence may not mean safer use.

Only the survey of 828 physicians in China examined staff in real deployment. Its structured-training estimate (AOR 22.2, 95% CI 1.6 to 305.6) rests on 15 people. The radiology tutorial did not change reading time. No study followed behavior in clinical workflows beyond the four-week follow-up in the nurse trial.

No test enrolled or reported on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Trained groups were clinicians and students in China, South Korea, Taiwan, Türkiye, and 39 other countries. No study examined how trained staff handle AI content for patients with language or literacy barriers.

Two supplied sources, the augmented intelligence principles and the CHAI guide, state that users must understand generative AI risks and limits. The remaining sources use should language. The NIST excerpt supplied addresses carbon offsets rather than training. None of the supplied sources is a statute or regulation, so the practice rests on voluntary guidance.

Programs ranged from a 45-minute session to a six-week course, and none reported cost or staff time. The 45-minute session raised acceptance and attitudes but did not change AI literacy (p=0.351). Surveys found that 94.4% of residents had no LLM training and 10.95% of students had formal instruction, so most systems would start with little existing training.

No study measured patient outcomes, patient trust, or whether trained staff disclosed AI use or connected patients to a human. Among Canadian medical students, 90.18% reported encountering inaccurate LLM information. Patients may therefore receive errors if staff rely on these tools without checking them.

commentary.research_gap: Controlled studies should compare trained and untrained clinicians in real deployment on observed outcomes. Useful outcomes include detection of fabricated or unlabeled AI content, verification behavior, and errors that reach patients. These studies need follow-up beyond one month and should report cost and staff time. They should also include safety-net settings and staff who serve patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the seven tests included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. All of them studied clinicians or students in academic or simulated settings, mostly outside the United States. Health systems that serve these populations therefore have no direct evidence on whether training changes how their staff use generative AI with patients.
